newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Shire says strategy reaps rewards.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Shire says strategy reaps rewards.

text.p: Tiny drug development group Shire Pharmaceuticals Plc said on Friday that its novel approach to building itself into a key player in the drugs industry was starting to pay off handsomely.
Shire, based in Andover, southern England, went into the black for only the second time in its ten-year history in the 12 months to June 30.
Figures published on Friday showed it made a pretax profit of 2.9 milllion stg, after losses of 7.0 million a year earlier, despite a doubling of research and development costs.
Sales leapt 244 percent to 21.0 million stg.
"It is a beautiful scenario for the full year," chief executive Rolf Stahel told Reuters in a telephone interview.
Shire is unusual in acquiring compounds after basic research has been done, developing them further and then seeking powerful marketing partners for its late-stage products.
It has 36 products already on the market, centred on calcium supplements and oestrogen replacement therapy.

Stahel said the turnaround in performance was due to three key factors -- a sharp rise in sales due to increased marketing, the acquisition of product development and licensing business SPC and royalty payments from Johnson & Johnson for Shire's Alzheimer's disease drug Galanthamine.
He said Shire's sales, which rose 28 percent to 7.3 million stg, grew "three times faster than market growth in the U.K."
He said the group's calcium products performed particularly strongly, stealing market share from majors like Sanofi and Sandoz AG. "We have walked on them and we are very proud of this," he said.

Shire boosted its sales force to 32 during the year, a progression Stahel said would continue as long as it was self-financing. "I don't want to make massive investments in marketing at the same time as R&D, that makes us like a biotech company and I don't want to be that," said Stahel.

Stahel said Shire, which floated on the stock exchange earlier this year and raised 20 million stg, will be run on a "broadly cash-neutral basis". Royalty payments from collaborators are a key element of the strategy.

Johnson & Johnson has paid Shire around eight million stg for Galanthamine since November 1995. The compound, derived from daffodil bulbs, is in Phase III trials for Alzheimer's, the fatal condition that causes dementia, and Phase II trials for chronic fatigue, or ME, where it has no competition.
Analysts beleive the compound could be on sale for Alzheimer's by 2000.
Stahel said Galanthamine will provide "very substantial income and has potential at the mega-drug level".

He also points to Lambda, used for preventing bone disease in patients with kidney disease, Sigma for treatment of the bone-wasting disease osteporosis, and Hyacne for treatment of acne as being potentially winning products.
All three compounds are now in the first stage of clinical trials.
